papers.title: User Preference-aware Fake News Detection
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 44th International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval
papers.method: UPFD: news root node plus user nodes (features from users' historical tweets) in a retweet tree; one GNN layer, readout, concatenation with the news embedding
papers.findings: Full text (TeX source): Table 2 already includes news-only baselines (BERT+MLP 71.04 / 85.76 acc, word2vec+MLP 76.47 / 84.61 on POL / GOS) against UPFD 84.62 / 97.23. Section 3.3 ablation '-EXO' removes all edges: accuracy 85.61 vs 81.63 on PolitiFact and 95.47 vs 93.92 on the second dataset (the text labels both sentences 'Politifact'). Five runs, t-test, 20/10/70 split.
papers.limitations: No standard deviations reported. The ablation's full model (GCNFN, word2vec, no news concatenation) reports 85.61, above the 80.54 for GCNFN with word2vec in Table 3; the difference is not explained.

papers.title: The Impact of Data Characteristics on GNN Evaluation for Detecting Fake News
papers.method: Five GNNs (GCN, GAT, GraphSAGE, GCNFN, GNNCL) against an MLP that mean-pools all node features; feature shuffling, edge rewiring and synthetic ego-graphs
papers.datasets: UPFD PolitiFact and GossipCop, BERT (768-d) features only
papers.findings: Full text (TeX source): stratified 10-fold CV, mean validation accuracy with 95% CI. Table 2: GossipCop GCNFN 96.1 +/- 1.6 vs MLP 90.8 +/- 3.0; PolitiFact GCNFN 82.7 +/- 5.5 vs MLP 74.3 +/- 7.4. Edge rewiring leaves accuracy above 90% on GossipCop; feature shuffling collapses GAT/GraphSAGE to chance while GCN and GNNCL keep about 80% on GossipCop, which the authors attribute to graph size or density. Over 75% of nodes are one hop from the root.
papers.limitations: Preprint, no code found (author portfolio lists it as a preprint). Text and table disagree: MLP on GossipCop 93.87% in text vs 90.8% in Table 2; MLP on PolitiFact 80.93% vs 74.3%; GAT on GossipCop 95.26% vs 91.5%. Reports validation accuracy only (no held-out test). The MLP pools user nodes too, so it does not separate news content from user features.

sections.summary: No-go for the proposal as written. Its core experiment, GNNs against a no-graph baseline on UPFD, is already in the UPFD paper (news-only baselines and an edge-removal ablation) [@dou2021upfd], in a 2025 preprint that benchmarks five GNNs against a same-feature MLP with confidence intervals, edge rewiring and feature shuffling [@karn2025structure], and in DAWN under temporal splits [@kim2025dawn]. The comparison as designed also could not isolate graph structure: this audit measured that most UPFD test graphs share Twitter users with training graphs, and a vote over those users' training labels, with no model, text or edges, reaches 75% on PolitiFact and 91% on GossipCop, close to published no-graph baselines. A revised question about what signal UPFD models actually use survives the novelty checks at low confidence and is a conditional go.

well_explored.text: GNN vs news-only or structure-agnostic baselines on UPFD, including edge removal, edge rewiring and feature shuffling
Content-only vs social-graph models under temporality-aware splits on FakeNewsNet
Adding explicit topology features to UPFD node features
New GNN architectures on UPFD (titles only screened among 186 citing works)

recommendation.text: Drop the proposal as written (no-go). Its answer is already published, and a rerun with more seeds would add little beyond [@karn2025structure].

Conditional go for the revised question (users shared between training and test). Proceed only if both checks below pass, which take about a week and need no training: (1) obtain and read [@bryla2026networks] and the two UPFD chapters [@rai2025attention; @rai2025hypergraph] through the university library and confirm none evaluates with user-disjoint splits or reports user overlap; (2) download the PolitiFact UPFD files (size not checked; the full two-dataset release is about 1.2 GB per the README, so ask before downloading GossipCop), confirm that a user has the same feature vector in every graph, and recompute the overlap on the official train/val/test index files.

If check 1 finds prior user-disjoint evaluation, fall back to the replication of Karn and Jensen or switch to the ABSA candidate from the opportunity report. If check 2 finds that user features differ per graph, the shortcut runs only through user overlap, not identical features, and the question narrows but remains open.

Whatever is chosen, do not compare against numbers from the official GNN-FakeNews script without rerunning: it ignores the fixed split files (random_split with seed 777), tests after the last epoch with no validation-based selection, uses max pooling where the paper says mean, sets weight decay 0.01 where the paper says 0.001, and averages macro-F1 over batches instead of computing it on the whole test set.

Framing risk: in social-context models, users shared across news are an intended signal [@nguyen2020fang]. Present the work as attributing performance to signals, not as exposing an error, unless the paper making a claim about structure or content is the one under test.

opportunities.title: As proposed: multi-seed graph vs no-graph re-evaluation of UPFD
opportunities.revision_note: Reading the full texts showed the experiment has been done three times: the UPFD paper itself reports news-only baselines and an edge-removal ablation [@dou2021upfd]; Karn and Jensen benchmark five GNNs against a same-feature MLP with 10-fold CIs, edge rewiring and feature shuffling on both UPFD datasets [@karn2025structure]; and DAWN compares a BERT content-only model with GNNs under temporal splits [@kim2025dawn]. A further multi-seed rerun would mainly confirm Karn and Jensen. The audit also found the comparison as designed cannot isolate graph structure (see the revised question).
opportunities.research_question: On UPFD PolitiFact and GossipCop, how much do GNNs over user-engagement graphs add beyond a classifier on news features alone, under 10+ seeds and repeated splits?
opportunities.motivation: Originally proposed as the top-ranked idea of the NLP+GNN opportunity report.

closest_existing_work.how_it_differs: Same question, same datasets and models, with an MLP on identical features, 10-fold CIs, edge rewiring and feature shuffling. Differs only in reporting validation rather than test accuracy and using BERT features only.
Already reports news-only MLP baselines and a no-edge ('-EXO') ablation, over five runs with t-tests.
Content-only BERT vs GNNs under a temporal split on raw FakeNewsNet rather than the UPFD release.

gap_evidence.text: UPFD Table 2 reports news-only baselines (BERT+MLP 71.04% / 85.76%) against UPFD (84.62% / 97.23%) on PolitiFact / GossipCop; the -EXO ablation removes all edges (85.61% vs 81.63% on PolitiFact)
An MLP on the same BERT node features reaches 90.8% +/- 3.0 vs 96.1% +/- 1.6 for GCNFN on GossipCop and 74.3% +/- 7.4 vs 82.7% +/- 5.5 on PolitiFact; edge rewiring leaves GossipCop accuracy above 90%
Under temporal splits a BERT content-only model reaches 84.2% on PolitiFact against 86.4% for GCN (5-run averages, no SD)

novelty.uncertainty: Rejected because the full texts of three papers describe the experiment. The tool's challenge searches returned 'no close match' both times and missed Karn and Jensen, which was found by web search; tool signals for this topic are unreliable.

opportunities.title: Revised: how much of UPFD performance comes from users shared between training and test graphs?
opportunities.revision_note: The original graph-vs-no-graph question is answered [@karn2025structure; @dou2021upfd]. While checking whether that comparison isolates structure, this audit measured that most UPFD test graphs share Twitter users with training graphs and that a model-free user vote reaches close to published accuracies. Neither the UPFD paper, Karn and Jensen, nor DAWN reports user overlap or a user-disjoint evaluation (checked in their full texts). The question was therefore moved from 'does the graph help' to 'what signal are UPFD models actually using'.
opportunities.research_question: How much of the accuracy of GNNs and of structure-agnostic baselines on UPFD depends on user identities shared between training and test graphs, and how much survives when that overlap is removed or controlled?
opportunities.motivation: Published comparisons on UPFD attribute performance to news content, user preferences or propagation structure [@dou2021upfd; @karn2025structure]. Every model that pools user-node features, including Karn and Jensen's MLP, can also exploit recurring users, and DAWN observes that users tend to engage with only one class [@kim2025dawn]. A review of fake news studies argues reported accuracies are shaped by evaluation design and possible leakage [@tuan2026review].

closest_existing_work.how_it_differs: Shuffles features and rewires edges but keeps user nodes, so a user-identity shortcut survives in every condition; uses random stratified folds without regard to users.

Temporal splits reduce future-information leakage and the paper notes users' label consistency, but it does not report user overlap between splits or a user-disjoint evaluation, and it uses raw FakeNewsNet rather than the UPFD release.
Treats users shared across news as intended social-context signal; the revised question would need to frame user reuse as a separate signal to measure, not as an error.
Unknown: title suggests a multi-dataset structural analysis; full text not obtained.

gap_evidence.text: Measured in this audit (script research-reports/upfd-audit/user_overlap.py, no model and no node features): 21.9% of PolitiFact user nodes and 78.6% of GossipCop user nodes belong to Twitter users who also appear in another graph; 81.5% (PolitiFact) and 60.4% (GossipCop) of those repeat users appear only in graphs of one label.

Labelling each test graph by the majority training label of its users (no text, no features, no edges; 20 random 20/10/70 splits as in the official script) gives accuracy 75.4% (SD 7.4, range 61.1-86.0) on PolitiFact and 91.1% (SD 1.0, range 89.5-92.9) on GossipCop; 98.9% (SD 0.1, range 98.6-99.1) of GossipCop test graphs share at least one user with training. Dropping users who appear in 50 or more graphs still gives 83.9% (SD 0.9, range 82.0-85.3) on GossipCop.

For comparison, published news-only baselines on UPFD reach 71.04-76.47% (PolitiFact) and 84.61-85.76% (GossipCop) [@dou2021upfd], and Karn and Jensen's MLP 74.3% and 90.8% [@karn2025structure]: the user vote alone is in the same range
Users tend to engage with either only fake or only real news (DAWN figure caption, raw FakeNewsNet)

Under feature shuffling, GCN and GNNCL still reach about 80% on GossipCop, which the authors attribute to graph size or density; news-node degree patterns are reported to indicate veracity [@wu2023decor]. Graph-level statistics are therefore a second shortcut that any decomposition must control.

If UPFD user features are per-user vectors (README: computed from each user's historical tweets), the same vector recurs across graphs and lets any feature-pooling model memorise users. Not checked: the feature files were not downloaded.

opportunities.contribution: An attribution audit of the most-used GNN fake-news benchmark: whether reported gains reflect news content, propagation structure or recurring users, with a reusable overlap measurement. Either outcome is reportable.

novelty.uncertainty: Two challenge searches and two web searches found no study of user overlap on UPFD, but the tool missed Karn and Jensen on the previous question, Semantic Scholar was rate-limited, and four UPFD-specific papers (two Springer chapters, a 2026 multi-dataset analysis, a Research Square preprint) could not be read. User-disjoint or inductive evaluation is also standard in neighbouring areas (recommendation, rumour detection) and may have been applied to FakeNewsNet under different wording.

opportunities.title: Fallback: independent replication of Karn and Jensen with a held-out test set
opportunities.research_question: Do Karn and Jensen's conclusions (MLP within a few points of GNNs; structure negligible) hold when measured on held-out test data, on the official UPFD split and with all four feature types, and which of their inconsistent reported numbers is correct?
opportunities.motivation: The paper is the closest and most recent evidence on the question, but it is an unreviewed preprint without code whose text and table disagree [@karn2025structure].

closest_existing_work.how_it_differs: The study being replicated; no code is available, so the project is a replication, not a reproduction.

gap_evidence.text: Text and Table 2 disagree (MLP on GossipCop 93.87% vs 90.8%; on PolitiFact 80.93% vs 74.3%; GAT on GossipCop 95.26% vs 91.5%)
Results are mean validation accuracy over 10 folds; no held-out test set is described

opportunities.contribution: A checked set of numbers for a claim others are likely to cite; low novelty.

novelty.uncertainty: A camera-ready version (the acknowledgements mention one) may already correct the inconsistencies; it was not found.

limitations: Novelty of the revised question rests on searches that missed the closest paper on the original question; treat it as unverified until the library check is done.
Not read (paywalled or no abstract): Bryla et al. 2026, Rai et al. 2025 (two chapters), Maurya et al. 2024. The DAWN appendix was not read.

The user-overlap diagnostic was run by this audit; it is a data measurement, not a reproduction. It used random 20/10/70 splits matching the official script, not the official index files, which were not downloaded.

Graph reconstruction assumes node ids are contiguous per graph with the news node first; this matched the released news list order and the paper's node totals, but was not checked against node_graph_id.npy.
Whether a user's feature vector is identical across graphs was not checked (feature files not downloaded).
Accounts appearing in thousands of GossipCop graphs were not identified; removing users in 50+ graphs lowered the GossipCop vote accuracy from 91.1% to 83.9%.
Karn and Jensen's text and table disagree; the audit quotes the table where it gives CIs and notes the conflict.
Semantic Scholar was rate-limited throughout; citing works came from OpenAlex and were screened by title only.
No model was trained and no published number was reproduced.
